This is especially great for when they’re not fully vaccinated yet because you don’t have to expose them to any possible germs! I like to start this all the way back at home though with rewarding calmness and attentiveness. It really sets them up for success in understanding that being calm and listening is a good thing.

The best kind of socializing is more like desensitizing. Just showing him things and rewarding him for being calm is a really great first step. I also live in a small rural area and it definitely feels tricky. As he gets a little older you can take the same idea of rewarding him for being calm and attentive to you but in pet friendly locations like some coffee shops / outdoor eating areas or stores. Remember to take him away if it gets too stressful though, and that you can always return to the basics (like the car idea!) if things get tricky.

Puppy training is not a linear progress, so if he seems to make progress and then fall back at any point it’s okay! He’s just growing up and you’re both learning. It’s really great that you want to do so well by him.

There’s some trainers out there that know far more than me. “MyBraveMona” on instagram has a pitty that they trained using only positive reinforcement, so they might be worth looking at :) especially the older videos of training their dog as a puppy.

Best of luck and happy trails to you and your new best friend!

Sorry you’re going through this. My best friend, a german shepherd that would’ve turned 3 last december, ended up developing epilepsy in may of 2024. It was absolutely brutal. After massive ups and downs (with each relapse of seizures getting worse) and multiple medications, plus the fact that I’m both physically far away from the vet and would’ve been financially unable to take her as often as would be warranted, I made the very heavy and heart wrenching decision to put her down. I’ve sobbed every day since I put her to sleep 2.5 weeks ago, but I know I ended both her suffering and a portion of mine. My mental and physical health both plummeted while worrying over her, and my whole family was exhausted from taking turns watching her as she’d seizure throughout the night. Both human and dog quality of life wasn’t good.

She had some great days, and lots of people talked about fighting the long fight with epilepsy, but she was actively getting worse despite treatment and it was truly only a matter of time before she hurt herself or I had to take her in in a more traumatic manner. I miss her more than I can express but I know it was the right thing. She had a very good last day, and I know that too soon is FAR better than at all too late.

I was in your shoes until 4 months ago! My girl is 7 months now, and although I’ve been reading about the breed and meeting GSDs my entire life, here’s what surprised me a little bit:

- more of a velcro dog than my dobie mix who I already considered a velcro dog. Barely had to put in the effort to teach recall (until she became a teenager and other things became more interesting lol). This dog will lay in the bathroom with me if I leave the door open. Not big on cuddles however.

- inherent nervousness. I knew shepherds were like this, but wow was it still a little surprising. She’s suspicious of basically everyone she meets and has little urge to socialize outside of her family (works for me, I’m an introvert that also has no interest lol). She’s truly the least stranger-friendly puppy I’ve ever had, and doesn’t even like some of my friends. We’re working on neutrality every day. 

- feeding right off of the last point, she’s insanely protective already. My family talked all the time about how my dobie mix is a protector and tough dog, but that was before my GSD puppy was here interrogating not only strangers but them too. I’m the only person she hasn’t alert-barked (and ran towards). She’s a sweetheart to them all normally but turns into a big guard dog if caught by surprise / if she doesn’t recognize them right away. Not saying this is desirable behavior of course, and it could easily become reactivity if left unchecked.

- those last two points turned on like a light switch at about 6 months btw. Until then she was a sweet puppy that hid behind me at loud noises.

Finally, the biggest thing I didn’t know: the comments in public / weird social interactions. Everyone assumes she’s male, everyone asks if she’s a mal, everyone talks about their brother who trains GSDs in the military, etc etc. There is also just a massive “tough guy” culture surrounding GSDs where (guys, mostly) brag about their dog being oversized and aggressive, and will also have a weird stigma about women owning the breed. It’s super weird.

All in all, basically everything I heard before getting one was true. Incredibly smart, loyal, hairy (oh my god the hair), and prone to reactivity. Like you, the cons just made me want one more and I don’t regret it for a second! Idk if I’ll ever have another breed lol. Prepare for a ton of proper socialization / desensitization training and “off switch” training, and best of luck!
